plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to take any company's balance sheet, say in plain words what it owns, what it owes and what is left for the owners, check that the two sides match, and spot three warning signs: more short-term debt than cash to cover it, a big pile of unpaid customer bills, and a growing gap between profit and cash.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14, you could compare two years of the same company's balance sheet and explain what changed and why.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28, you could read a balance sheet alongside the income statement and cash flow statement and tell a short story of the business from all three.

picture.name: A house with a mortgage
picture.line: A balance sheet is a photo of one house on one day: the house and everything in it is what you own, the mortgage and the unpaid bills are what you owe, and whatever is left is yours.

chapters.title: The one equation
chapters.covers: Own minus owe equals yours: assets, liabilities and equity, and why the two sides of the sheet always add up to the same number.
chapters.outcome: You can take any balance sheet, find the three totals, and show that what it owns equals what it owes plus what belongs to the owners.
chapters.hook: A balance sheet always balances. That is less reassuring than it sounds.

chapters.title: A photo, not a film
chapters.covers: A balance sheet shows one day, not a year; where the date sits, how it differs from an income statement, and why two dates side by side matter.
chapters.outcome: You can say which day a balance sheet describes and explain why it cannot tell you how much the company earned.
chapters.hook: Why does cash sit at the top of the page and the factory at the bottom?

chapters.title: What it owns: assets, fast and slow
chapters.covers: Current assets that turn to cash within 12 months (cash, stock, bills customers owe) versus long-term ones (buildings, machines, brands bought from others).
chapters.outcome: You can sort every asset line into fast or slow and name the two or three biggest things the company owns.
chapters.hook: A company can have millions in the bank and still miss next month's payroll.

chapters.title: What it owes: debts, soon and later
chapters.covers: Current liabilities due within 12 months (supplier bills, short-term loans, taxes) versus long-term debt, and reading the amounts and due dates.
chapters.outcome: You can list what the company must pay in the next 12 months and what it can pay later, and name who it owes.
chapters.hook: Billions in retained earnings can sit right beside an almost empty bank account.

chapters.title: What is left: the owners' share
chapters.covers: Equity as money the owners put in plus profit kept over the years, why it can shrink or go negative, and why it is not the same as what the company is worth.
chapters.outcome: You can explain where the equity number came from and say whether past profits were kept or paid out.
chapters.hook: The most important thing on the page is a date, and most people skip it.

chapters.title: Three checks in five minutes
chapters.covers: Three quick comparisons: current assets against current liabilities, total debt against equity, and cash against short-term debt; what a healthy and an unhealthy number looks like.
chapters.outcome: You can run the three checks on a real balance sheet and say in one sentence whether the company can pay its bills this year.
chapters.hook: Two subtractions and one division tell you if a company can pay its bills.

chapters.title: Reading a real one, start to finish
chapters.covers: A full walk through a published balance sheet from a listed company: the order of lines, the footnotes, the odd items, and the three warning signs to look for.
chapters.outcome: You can read a real published balance sheet in 20 minutes and tell someone else what the company owns, owes, and whether anything worries you.
chapters.hook: The most valuable thing many companies own is nowhere on the page.

hooksFrom.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to open any public company's balance sheet, say in plain words what each line means, and answer three questions from it: what the company owns, what it owes, and whether it can pay its bills in the next 12 months.
hooksFrom.horizon14: Later: put two companies from the same industry side by side and say which one carries more debt, and why that matters.
hooksFrom.horizon28: Later still: read the balance sheet next to the income statement and cash flow statement and notice when the three tell different stories.

picture.name: A family's money on one day
picture.line: A balance sheet is a photo of one family's finances taken on a single day: the house and the savings on one side, the mortgage and the credit card on the other, and whatever is left is truly theirs.

chapters.title: The one sentence the whole page obeys
chapters.covers: What you own, minus what you owe, is what's yours. Why the two sides always add up to the same number, using a family with a house, a car, savings and a mortgage.
chapters.outcome: You can sort 10 everyday items into own, owe or yours, and explain why both sides of a balance sheet always match.
chapters.hook: A balance sheet always balances. That is less reassuring than it sounds.

chapters.title: What the company owns, top to bottom
chapters.covers: The assets side: cash, money customers still owe, stock on shelves, buildings and machines. Why the list runs from easiest-to-spend at the top to hardest-to-sell at the bottom, and what 'current' means (turns into cash within 12 months).
chapters.outcome: You can read the assets side of a real balance sheet and say which items could become cash within a year and which could not.
chapters.hook: Why does cash sit at the top of the page and the factory at the bottom?

chapters.title: What the company owes, and when
chapters.covers: The liabilities side: unpaid supplier bills, wages owed, short-term loans, long-term loans. The one split that matters most: what is due within 12 months versus later. The family version: this month's credit card bill versus the 25-year mortgage.
chapters.outcome: You can find the total a company must pay within 12 months and compare it to the cash and near-cash it has.
chapters.hook: A company can have millions in the bank and still miss next month's payroll.

chapters.title: What's left: the owners' slice
chapters.covers: Equity: money the owners put in, plus profits kept back over the years. Why 'retained earnings' is a running tally, not a pile of cash. The family version: the house is worth 400, the mortgage is 300, so the family's slice is 100, even though they hold no 100 in hand.
chapters.outcome: You can explain what equity is, where it comes from, and why a large equity number does not mean the company has that money available.
chapters.hook: Billions in retained earnings can sit right beside an almost empty bank account.

chapters.title: Reading a real one, line by line
chapters.covers: Open an actual public company's balance sheet from its annual report. The date at the top, the two columns (this year and last year), the units line (thousands or millions), the subtotals, and the footnote references. Walk the whole page once, slowly.
chapters.outcome: You can take an unfamiliar balance sheet and walk it top to bottom, naming each section and reading the units correctly.
chapters.hook: The most important thing on the page is a date, and most people skip it.

chapters.title: Three quick checks with a calculator
chapters.covers: Working capital (current assets minus current liabilities), the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities), and debt compared to equity. What a result of 1.5 or 0.8 means in plain words, and why none of these is a verdict on its own.
chapters.outcome: You can compute three checks from any balance sheet and say what each one suggests about the company's ability to pay its bills and how much it relies on borrowing.
chapters.hook: Two subtractions and one division tell you if a company can pay its bills.

chapters.title: What the photo leaves out
chapters.covers: The limits: it is one day, not a year. Buildings are shown at what they cost, not what they're worth today. A brand built in-house usually does not appear at all. Why the balance sheet needs the income statement (the year's earnings) and the cash flow statement (where the cash actually went) beside it.
chapters.outcome: You can name four things a balance sheet cannot tell you and say which other statement you would open to find each one.
chapters.hook: The most valuable thing many companies own is nowhere on the page.
